gloss: A system of raised dots that blind people read with their fingers.
examples: The elevator buttons have *braille* next to the numbers.
She learned *braille* after losing her sight at twelve.
The museum offers labels in *braille* and in large print.

gloss: The lower part of the brain that joins it to the spinal cord and controls breathing and heartbeat.
examples: The tumor was pressing on his *brainstem*.
Damage to the *brainstem* can stop a person from breathing.
The scan showed no injury to the *brainstem*.

gloss: The act of forcing someone to accept new beliefs through pressure and repetition.
examples: The documentary describes the cult's *brainwashing* of new members.
He calls most advertising a mild form of *brainwashing*.
Years of *brainwashing* had left her afraid to ask questions.

gloss: The rough outer layer of a grain, removed when white flour is made.
examples: He eats *bran* cereal every morning for the fiber.
The recipe calls for a cup of oat *bran*.
White bread has had the *bran* stripped out of it.

gloss: A woman's undergarment that supports the breasts.
examples: The label on the package said *brassiere*, size 34B.
Department stores still list them as *brassieres* in the catalog.
She bought a nursing *brassiere* before the baby came.
contrast: Formal and old-fashioned; Americans say *bra* in ordinary speech. The -iere spelling hides a plain bruh-ZEER.

gloss: A show of courage meant to impress, hiding real fear.
examples: His threats were pure *bravado* and everyone knew it.
There was a lot of *bravado* in the locker room before the game.
Beneath the *bravado* he was terrified of losing.

gloss: A noisy, rough fight involving several people.
examples: A *brawl* broke out in the parking lot after the concert.
Two players were ejected for starting a bench-clearing *brawl*.
Police broke up several *brawls* downtown that night.

gloss: Physical strength, especially muscle.
examples: The job takes brains as much as *brawn*.
He had the *brawn* to carry the freezer up two flights of stairs.
All that *brawn* was no help when the truck wouldn't start.

gloss: A tiny piece of bread, often dried and used to coat food before frying.
examples: Dip the chicken in egg, then roll it in *breadcrumbs*.
A single *breadcrumb* was all that was left on the plate.
She scattered *breadcrumbs* on the path for the ducks.
contrast: The b in crumb is silent: BRED-krum.

gloss: A long thin stick of baked bread served before or with a meal.
examples: The restaurant brings out warm *breadsticks* while you wait.
He ate a whole *breadstick* before the soup arrived.
Order the salad and *breadsticks* — they're unlimited.

gloss: The person in a family who earns the money the others live on.
examples: After the layoff, she became the family's only *breadwinner*.
In many households both parents are *breadwinners*.
He felt the pressure of being the *breadwinner* at twenty-three.

gloss: Damage caused by things being broken, or the amount of such damage.
examples: The shipping insurance covers *breakage* in transit.
Wrap each glass separately to prevent *breakage*.
The store loses about two percent a year to *breakage*.

gloss: An important discovery or advance that solves a stubborn problem.
examples: The vaccine was a major *breakthrough* in public health.
After months of therapy she finally had a *breakthrough*.
The lab has reported two *breakthroughs* this year.

gloss: A swimming stroke in which the arms sweep forward and the legs kick like a frog's.
examples: She swims the *breaststroke* faster than anyone on the team.
He won gold in the 100-meter *breaststroke*.
The class covers freestyle, backstroke, and *breaststroke*.
contrast: The first part rhymes with *rest*: BREST-strohk, not 'breest'.

gloss: The act of taking air into the lungs and letting it out.
examples: Her *breathing* got slower as she fell asleep.
The nurse checked his pulse and *breathing*.
Deep *breathing* helps me calm down before a test.
contrast: Long ee with a voiced th: BREE-thing. The noun *breath* is short and hissed: /brɛθ/, BRETH.

gloss: Short trousers that fasten just below the knee, worn for riding or in period costume.
examples: The riders wore white *breeches* and black boots.
His costume included a wig and velvet *breeches*.
A pair of leather *breeches* hung by the stable door.
contrast: Said BRICH-iz, not 'breech-ez'. Always plural, like *pants* — a pair of *breeches*.

gloss: Shortness, especially of speech or writing.
examples: For the sake of *brevity*, I'll skip the background.
The memo was admired for its *brevity*.
*Brevity* is the soul of wit.

gloss: A person or company that makes beer.
examples: He worked as a *brewer* in Portland for ten years.
The country's largest *brewer* is raising prices again.
Local *brewers* set up tents along the river.

gloss: A bar or restaurant that brews its own beer on the premises.
examples: There's a new *brewpub* on Third Street.
We had burgers at a *brewpub* downtown.
The town has three *brewpubs* within a few blocks.

gloss: A prickly bush, or one of its thorny stems.
examples: The dog came back with *briars* stuck in its fur.
A thick *briar* had grown across the trail.
We cut back the *briars* along the fence line.
contrast: Also spelled *brier*; both are said BRY-ur.

gloss: A worker who builds walls and other structures out of bricks.
examples: His grandfather was a *bricklayer* in Chicago.
The contractor hired two more *bricklayers* for the job.
A good *bricklayer* can set hundreds of bricks a day.

gloss: A soft, mild French cheese with a white rind.
examples: She served *brie* with crackers and green apples.
Warm the *brie* in the oven for ten minutes.
There's half a wheel of *brie* left in the fridge.

gloss: Short, close-fitting underpants with no legs.
examples: He bought a three-pack of cotton *briefs*.
The store sells boxers, *briefs*, and boxer briefs.
A clean pair of *briefs* was all he had left in the bag.
contrast: Always plural, like *pants*: a pair of *briefs*, never 'a brief' in this sense.

gloss: Great brightness, or unusually great intelligence and skill.
examples: No one doubted the *brilliance* of her argument.
The *brilliance* of the stage lights made him squint.
There are flashes of *brilliance* in his early work.

gloss: The very edge of something, especially of a dangerous situation.
examples: The company was on the *brink* of bankruptcy.
They pulled back from the *brink* at the last minute.
She stood at the *brink* of the canyon and looked down.

gloss: The tactic of pushing a dangerous situation to the edge to force the other side to give in.
examples: The budget fight was another round of *brinkmanship*.
Voters are tired of *brinkmanship* over the debt ceiling.
His *brinkmanship* nearly wrecked the negotiations.

gloss: A light, sweet French bread made with butter and eggs.
examples: The burger comes on a *brioche* bun.
She picked up two *brioches* at the bakery.
French toast is best made with day-old *brioche*.

gloss: A small block of pressed charcoal or coal used as fuel.
examples: Pile the *briquettes* in a pyramid before lighting them.
One bag of *briquettes* lasts us the whole summer.
Wait until the *briquettes* turn gray before you start grilling.

gloss: The business or activity of sending out programs on radio and television.
examples: She studied *broadcasting* at Northwestern.
Public *broadcasting* depends on donations from viewers.
He spent forty years in *broadcasting*.

gloss: A firm that buys and sells stocks, property, or insurance for clients.
examples: He opened an account at an online *brokerage*.
Several *brokerages* cut their price targets for the stock.
The *brokerage* charges no fee for stock trades.

gloss: A wild or half-tamed horse of the American West.
examples: He was thrown by a *bronco* at the rodeo.
The ranch still breaks *broncos* the old way.
Riding a bucking *bronco* takes eight seconds of nerve.

gloss: The long handle of a broom, or the whole broom a witch is imagined riding.
examples: The witch costume came with a plastic *broomstick*.
He propped the door open with a *broomstick*.
Kids raced around the yard on *broomsticks*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A feeling of closeness among people, or an organized group whose members treat one another as brothers.
examples: The team was held together by a real sense of *brotherhood*.
His father belonged to a railroad workers' *brotherhood*.
Several *brotherhoods* marched together in the parade.

gloss: A small square of dense, chewy chocolate cake.
examples: She brought a pan of *brownies* to the potluck.
I'll take a *brownie* and a glass of milk.
These *brownies* are still warm from the oven.

gloss: The heaviest part of something bad, such as an attack or a storm.
examples: Coastal towns took the *brunt* of the hurricane.
Younger workers bore the *brunt* of the layoffs.
She took the *brunt* of her boss's anger.

gloss: Cruel, violent treatment of people.
examples: The report documents police *brutality* in several cities.
He described the *brutality* of the prison camp.
The film does not hide the *brutality* of the war.

gloss: A grain-like seed used for flour and porridge, and the plant it comes from.
examples: Sunday mornings we make *buckwheat* pancakes.
The field behind the barn is planted with *buckwheat*.
Soba noodles are made from *buckwheat* flour.

gloss: Someone who knows a lot about a subject and follows it as a hobby.
examples: My uncle is a Civil War *buff*.
Film *buffs* will recognize the reference right away.
You don't have to be a wine *buff* to enjoy this bottle.

gloss: Something placed between two things to soften the effect of one on the other.
examples: Savings act as a *buffer* against unexpected bills.
A row of trees serves as a *buffer* between the road and the houses.
The agreement created a *buffer* zone along the border.

gloss: A small light vehicle, such as a horse-drawn carriage or an open off-road car.
examples: An Amish *buggy* was moving slowly down the shoulder.
They rented a dune *buggy* for the afternoon.
Two *buggies* were parked outside the general store.

gloss: A small brass horn with no valves, used to sound military signals.
examples: A *bugle* played Taps at the graveside.
Camp started every morning with a *bugle*.
The museum has two Civil War *bugles* on display.

gloss: Cracked wheat that has been steamed and dried, used in salads and side dishes.
examples: Tabbouleh is made with *bulgur*, parsley, and lemon.
Soak the *bulgur* in hot water for twenty minutes.
We keep *bulgur* and couscous in the pantry.

gloss: An eating disorder in which a person overeats and then vomits or otherwise avoids gaining weight.
examples: She was treated for *bulimia* in college.
*Bulimia* often goes unnoticed for years.
The clinic specializes in anorexia and *bulimia*.

gloss: A public event in which a matador fights and usually kills a bull.
examples: We went to a *bullfight* in Seville.
Tickets to the *bullfight* sold out in a day.
*Bullfights* are banned in some Spanish regions.

gloss: The sport or tradition of fighting bulls in an arena.
examples: *Bullfighting* has lost popularity with younger Spaniards.
Animal rights groups campaign against *bullfighting*.
He wrote a whole book about *bullfighting*.

gloss: Gold or silver in the form of bars, valued by weight.
examples: The vault holds several tons of gold *bullion*.
Investors have been buying silver *bullion* all year.
The coins sell at the *bullion* price plus a small fee.
contrast: Not *bouillon* /ˈbuːjɑːn/ (BOO-yahn), which is broth.

gloss: Nonsense or lies — a very common but vulgar word.
examples: His excuse was complete *bullshit*.
I'm tired of listening to corporate *bullshit*.
She called *bullshit* on the whole story.
contrast: Vulgar. Fine among friends, never in class, an interview, or writing for work.

gloss: Someone who repeatedly frightens or hurts weaker people.
examples: A *bully* on the bus took his lunch money.
Most *bullies* back down when you stand up to them.
She refused to let a *bully* run her classroom.

gloss: Repeated cruel treatment of someone weaker, especially at school or work.
examples: The school has a strict policy on *bullying*.
Online *bullying* follows kids home now.
She reported the *bullying* to her manager.

gloss: An informal word for a disappointing or annoying situation.
examples: Rain on your birthday — what a *bummer*.
It's a *bummer* that the concert got canceled.
The flat tire was the first of several *bummers* that day.

gloss: A thick elastic cord, used to strap down loads or to jump from a height.
examples: He strapped the cooler down with a *bungee*.
She went *bungee* jumping in New Zealand.
A pack of *bungees* costs about ten dollars.

ru: шишка (косточка) у основания большого пальца ноги
gloss: A painful swollen bump at the base of the big toe.
examples: Tight shoes made her *bunion* worse.
He had surgery on both *bunions* last spring.
The podiatrist said the *bunion* was hereditary.

gloss: In baseball, a hit made by holding the bat still so the ball rolls a short distance.
examples: He laid down a perfect *bunt* to move the runner over.
The third baseman charged in to field the *bunt*.
Two *bunts* in a row caught the defense off guard.

gloss: The ability of an object to float, or the upward push a liquid gives it.
examples: Salt water gives swimmers extra *buoyancy*.
The vest adds enough *buoyancy* to keep a child afloat.
We measured the *buoyancy* of each block in the tank.

gloss: A heavy load, or a difficult duty or worry someone has to carry.
examples: Caring for both parents became a real *burden*.
The new tax shifts the *burden* onto small businesses.
He carried the *burden* of the secret for years.

gloss: A style of stage entertainment mixing comedy, song, and striptease.
examples: The theater started out as a *burlesque* house in the 1920s.
She performs *burlesque* on weekends.
The show is a modern take on old-fashioned *burlesque*.

gloss: A loose garment worn by some Muslim women that covers the whole body and face.
examples: Several countries have banned the *burqa* in public buildings.
She wore a blue *burqa* in the photograph.
The rules on *burqas* vary from region to region.

gloss: A sudden short outbreak of sound, energy, or activity.
examples: There was a *burst* of applause when she finished.
He works in short *bursts* and then takes a break.
A *burst* of wind knocked the umbrella over.

gloss: A man who works in business, especially at a senior level.
examples: Her father was a *businessman* who traveled constantly.
Two *businessmen* were arguing in the hotel lobby.
He presents himself as a self-made *businessman*.
contrast: The plural *businessmen* is said BIZ-nis-men. Use *businessperson* when the gender is unknown.

gloss: Noisy, busy movement of people in a place.
examples: I miss the *bustle* of the city.
The kitchen was full of *bustle* an hour before service.
They wanted a quiet town away from all the *bustle*.
contrast: The t is silent: BUS-uhl, like *hustle* and *whistle*.

ru: назойливый человек, любитель совать нос в чужие дела
gloss: Someone who is too interested in other people's private affairs.
examples: The neighborhood *busybody* watches everyone's driveway.
Don't be such a *busybody*.
A couple of *busybodies* had already called the police.

gloss: Tasks given to keep people occupied rather than to accomplish anything.
examples: The substitute handed out *busywork* all afternoon.
Most of my first week was *busywork*.
Cut the *busywork* and let the team do real work.

gloss: Someone whose job is cutting up and selling meat.
examples: Ask the *butcher* to trim the fat off.
There's a good *butcher* two blocks over.
The *butchers* start work at four in the morning.

gloss: The chief male servant of a large household.
examples: The *butler* answered the door.
In the movie, the *butler* did it.
The estate once employed two *butlers* and a cook.

gloss: An informal word for the part of the body you sit on.
examples: Get off your *butt* and help me.
He slipped on the ice and landed on his *butt*.
The jeans were too tight in the *butt*.

gloss: A steep, isolated hill with a flat top, common in the American West.
examples: A red *butte* rose out of the desert ahead of us.
We camped at the base of the *butte*.
The highway runs between two sandstone *buttes*.
contrast: Rhymes with *cute*: BYOOT, not like *butt*.

gloss: A small wild plant with shiny yellow cup-shaped flowers.
examples: The field was covered in *buttercups*.
She tucked a *buttercup* behind her ear.
*Buttercups* come up every May along the ditch.

gloss: A sweet flavor or candy made from butter and brown sugar.
examples: He ordered the sundae with *butterscotch* sauce.
There's a bowl of *butterscotch* candies by the register.
The pudding tastes like *butterscotch*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A low humming sound, or excited talk about something new.
examples: There's a lot of *buzz* about her new album.
I heard a *buzz* and found a wasp at the window.
The refrigerator makes strange *buzzes* at night.

gloss: An electric device that makes a buzzing sound as a signal.
examples: Press the *buzzer* and I'll let you in.
He scored right before the *buzzer*.
The contestants each have a *buzzer* in front of them.

gloss: A fashionable word or phrase used to sound impressive, often with little real meaning.
examples: Synergy is the *buzzword* everyone hates.
His presentation was nothing but *buzzwords*.
Every year a new *buzzword* takes over the industry.

gloss: A rule a club, company, or association makes to govern itself.
examples: The homeowners' association changed its *bylaws* last year.
That's against the club's *bylaws*.
A *bylaw* requires two weeks' notice before any vote.

gloss: A small shelter beside a pool or beach, used for changing or for shade.
examples: We rented a *cabana* by the pool for the day.
The hotel has a dozen *cabanas* along the beach.
She changed into her swimsuit in the *cabana*.

gloss: A dry red wine made from Cabernet Sauvignon grapes.
examples: He ordered a glass of *cabernet* with his steak.
This *cabernet* is from Napa Valley.
I prefer a *cabernet* to a merlot.
contrast: The final t is silent: kab-ur-NAY.

gloss: A skilled woodworker who makes fine furniture and cabinets.
examples: A local *cabinetmaker* built the kitchen island.
He apprenticed with a *cabinetmaker* for four years.
The best *cabinetmakers* still cut dovetails by hand.

gloss: The seeds, and the tree they grow on, that chocolate and cocoa are made from.
examples: The bar is 70 percent *cacao*.
*Cacao* grows only near the equator.
She adds raw *cacao* to her smoothies.

gloss: The prestige or special appeal that comes from being widely admired.
examples: An Ivy League degree still carries some *cachet*.
The brand lost its *cachet* once everyone had one.
There's a certain *cachet* to a handwritten letter.
contrast: French spelling, silent t: ka-SHAY.

gloss: A harsh mixture of loud, clashing sounds.
examples: The market was a *cacophony* of shouting and car horns.
A *cacophony* rose from the orchestra pit as they tuned up.
Outside there was nothing but the *cacophony* of construction.

gloss: A dead human body, especially one used for medical study.
examples: First-year students work on a *cadaver* in anatomy lab.
The school receives *cadavers* through a donation program.
He fainted the first time he saw a *cadaver*.

gloss: The rhythm and rise and fall of speech, music, or movement.
examples: You can hear a Southern *cadence* in her speech.
The soldiers marched to a steady *cadence*.
His sentences fall into long, careful *cadences*.

gloss: A young person training to become an officer in the military or the police.
examples: Her son is a *cadet* at West Point.
The *cadets* lined up for inspection at dawn.
He spent two years as a police *cadet*.

gloss: Something very easy to do.
examples: The final exam was a *cakewalk*.
Don't expect the second round to be a *cakewalk*.
Compared to last year's climb, this one was a *cakewalk*.

gloss: An event that causes great damage or suffering.
examples: The flood was the worst *calamity* in the town's history.
One *calamity* followed another that winter.
He warned of economic *calamity* if the bill passed.

gloss: The process of working something out with numbers, or the result of it.
examples: A quick *calculation* showed we were short by fifty dollars.
Check your *calculations* before you submit the form.
By my *calculation*, the trip will take nine hours.

gloss: Simple exercises such as push-ups and jumping jacks, done without equipment.
examples: The class starts with ten minutes of *calisthenics*.
*Calisthenics* is all he does — no weights at all.
Basic training includes daily *calisthenics*.
contrast: Looks plural but takes a singular verb: *calisthenics* is good for you.

gloss: A person who makes a telephone call.
examples: The *caller* hung up without leaving a message.
Our next *caller* is on the line from Denver.
*Caller* ID showed an unknown number.

gloss: A person skilled at beautiful decorative handwriting.
examples: They hired a *calligrapher* to address the wedding invitations.
The *calligrapher* worked with a steel nib and black ink.
Several *calligraphers* were demonstrating at the fair.

gloss: The state of being quiet, steady, and not upset.
examples: Her *calmness* during the emergency impressed everyone.
He answered with surprising *calmness*.
There was a strange *calmness* in the room after the news.
contrast: The l is silent: KAHM-nis, like *calm* and *palm*.

gloss: A portable video camera that records onto tape or a memory card.
examples: Dad filmed every recital on his old *camcorder*.
We found a box of *camcorder* tapes in the attic.
Phones have mostly replaced the family *camcorder*.

gloss: An evergreen shrub with glossy leaves and large pink, red, or white flowers.
examples: A *camellia* blooms outside her kitchen window every February.
The garden club is giving away *camellia* cuttings.
He planted three *camellias* along the north wall.

gloss: A soft, creamy French cheese with a white rind, sold in small rounds.
examples: We baked a round of *camembert* with honey and thyme.
The cheese plate had *camembert*, blue, and cheddar.
*Camembert* smells stronger than brie.
contrast: The final t is silent: KAM-uhm-bair.

gloss: A man who operates a film or television camera.
examples: The *cameraman* kept the shot steady through the whole take.
Two *cameramen* were injured covering the protest.
He started as a *cameraman* at a local news station.
contrast: The plural *cameramen* is said KAM-ruh-men. *Camera operator* is the gender-neutral term.

gloss: A light sleeveless top with thin straps, worn as underwear or on its own.
examples: She wore a silk *camisole* under the blazer.
The store had *camisoles* in six colors.
Pack a *camisole* or two for warm evenings.

gloss: A white substance with a strong smell, used in chest rubs and moth repellents.
examples: The ointment smells of *camphor* and menthol.
*Camphor* keeps moths out of a wool closet.
She rubbed a little *camphor* on his chest before bed.

gloss: The act of calling off something that was planned, or an instance of it.
examples: The snowstorm caused hundreds of flight *cancellations*.
There's a fee for *cancellation* within 24 hours.
We got a table thanks to a last-minute *cancellation*.
contrast: Two l's here, even though American English spells the verb *canceled* with one.

gloss: A tall branched holder for several candles.
examples: A silver *candelabrum* stood in the middle of the table.
The dining room was lit by two *candelabra*.
She polished the *candelabrum* before the guests arrived.
contrast: Latin plural: one *candelabrum*, several *candelabra*.

gloss: The soft light given off by burning candles.
examples: We ate dinner by *candlelight* during the outage.
The room looked warmer in *candlelight*.
A *candlelight* vigil was held outside the courthouse.
